props.title: Rubber
props.initialSlug: A killer tire rolls through town on a psychic rampage

sections.content: **Rubber** (2010) stands as one of cinema's most audacious experiments in meta-commentary and absurdist storytelling. Director Quentin Dupieux crafts a deliberately bizarre tale about a telepathic killer tire named Robert, while simultaneously forcing viewers to question the very nature of watching films. It shares DNA with self-aware classics like **Adaptation** (2002) and **Funny Games** (1997), but pushes even further into pure surrealism. The film's "no reason" philosophy, explicitly stated in its opening monologue, connects to broader traditions of French absurdist theater and the anti-art Dada movement. Rubber|2010|A sentient tire named Robert discovers psychic powers and goes on a killing spree while an audience watches the events unfold through binoculars|Tubi Wrong|2012|A man searches for his lost dog in increasingly bizarre circumstances, directed by Rubber's Quentin Dupieux|Prime Video Deerskin|2019|A man becomes obsessed with his designer deerskin jacket, which he believes gives him special powers|HBO Max

Dupieux's follow-up films continue exploring similar territory of reality-bending narratives. **Wrong** (2012) and **Reality** (2014) build on Rubber's foundation of questioning what makes sense in storytelling. These films, along with **Deerskin** (2019), form a loose trilogy of absurdist character studies where seemingly ordinary objects take on extraordinary significance. The influence of directors like David Lynch, particularly **Mulholland Drive** (2001), and Charlie Kaufman's **Synecdoche, New York** (2008) is evident in how Dupieux layers reality upon reality. SUBHEAD: Breaking the Fourth Wall in Modern Cinema

Rubber's unique approach to breaking the fourth wall - having an actual audience within the film watching and commenting on events - creates a fascinating dialogue with other meta-films. While **The Purple Rose of Cairo** (1985) had characters stepping out of the screen and **Last Action Hero** (1993) played with movie reality versus actual reality, Rubber takes the concept further by making the audience complicit in the narrative. This technique resurfaces in films like **Cabin in the Woods** (2012), where viewers must question their own role in consuming violence as entertainment.
